subject: Climate & Environment
title: Urban Forests and Cooling
description: A short lesson to help you apply Urban Forests and Cooling.

hook.text: A single mature tree can cool a neighborhood as much as 10 air conditioners running 20 hours.

buildup.text: Trees provide shade and release water through transpiration, cooling the air around them.

discovery.text: Cities with robust tree canopies can be 5 to 8°C cooler than treeless neighborhoods nearby.

twist.text: Many cities are losing trees to development, disease, and storms faster than they plant new ones.

climax.text: Urban tree planting programs are among the cheapest and most effective heat mitigation strategies.

punchline.text: The best air conditioner on Earth grows from a seed.

quiz.question: How much cooler can tree-covered neighborhoods be compared to treeless ones?

details.summary: Urban forests and street trees cool cities by providing shade and releasing water through transpiration, lowering air temperatures by up to 8 degrees Celsius in dense canopy areas. They also filter pollutants, absorb CO2, reduce stormwater runoff, and improve mental health for residents.
details.whyItMatters: As heat waves intensify, urban tree canopy is a low-cost, high-impact cooling strategy. Every tree planted today provides growing benefits for decades as cities warm.
takeaways: Trees can cool surrounding air by up to 8 degrees Celsius
They filter air pollutants and absorb carbon dioxide
Urban forests reduce stormwater runoff and flood risk

faq.question: How do trees cool cities?
faq.answer: Trees cool through two mechanisms: shading surfaces that would otherwise absorb and radiate heat, and evapotranspiration, where trees release water vapor from leaves, absorbing heat from the air. A single mature tree can transpire hundreds of liters per day.

faq.question: What is the urban heat island effect?
faq.answer: Cities are several degrees warmer than surrounding rural areas because dark surfaces like asphalt and concrete absorb and reradiate solar heat, vehicles and buildings add waste heat, and limited vegetation reduces natural cooling. Trees directly counteract this effect.
